title: Join second ‘Music Now! Musica Nostra!’ Forum in Mafra, Portugal, drawing a thread between music, heritage and climate change
content:
The ‘Music Now! Musica Nostra!’ Forum is returning to Mafra. Taking place at the Royal Building of Mafra from 7-8 November 2026, the gathering will bring together leading European figures and experts from the fields of music, heritage, science, the environment and civil society, alongside youth representatives, around a shared ambition: to make music and listening catalysts for passing on heritage, fostering dialogue and strengthening European cohesion.

Organised by Hub partner Centre Européen de Musique, ‘Music Now! Musica Nostra!’ is held in the frame of the EU-funded European Heritage Hub, in collaboration with Europa Nostra, the Municipality of Mafra, and partner Centro Nacional de Cultura, which oversees the Europa Nostra Heritage Hub in Lisbon. The event is placed under the High Patronage of the President of the French Republic. Visits to cultural sites will also take place, thanks to the Museus e Monumentos de Portugal and Museu Nacional da Musica.

title: First Intergenerational Climate Conversation at Sagres Promontory connects cultural and natural heritage with climate adaptation
content:
The first Intergenerational Climate Conversation, held on 5-6 October 2026 at the European Heritage Label site of Sagres Promontory, Portugal, brought together heritage professionals, researchers, locals and participants from different generations to explore how cultural and natural heritage can adapt to a changing climate.

Organised within the framework of the EU-funded European Heritage Hub by ICLEI Europe, together with Project Leader Europa Nostra and partners Youth.Heritage.Europe. and the European Heritage Label Bureau, the event explored the connections between climate, biodiversity, traditional knowledge and cultural memory, asking what must be protected today to ensure that heritage remains meaningful for future generations.

Sagres provided a fitting setting for the conversation, as a place deeply connected to Portugal’s maritime history and natural environment.

title: Youth.Heritage.Europe. brings youth voices to third Policy Debate on responsible tourism and heritage
content:
How can cultural tourism support heritage conservation without placing additional pressure on the places and communities it celebrates? This question guided Youth.Heritage.Europe.’s third Youth Policy Debate, organised within the frame of the EU-funded European Heritage Hub.

With welcoming remarks from Jasna Popović, Secretary of Youth.Heritage.Europe, and a panel moderated by Sophia Dibbs, Youth.Heritage.Europe.’s Programmes Officer, the event on 30 September 2026 brought together Chiara Ronchini, Theo Alexandridis, Daphne Gerodimou, and Andrea Bringas to discuss responsible tourism and the role of young people in shaping heritage practices.

The discussion explored the tensions between attracting visitors, protecting heritage, and maintaining the quality of life of local residents. Theo Alexandridis, one of the Hub’s NextGen Heritage Ambassadors, outlined environmental deterioration, physical damage, and social displacement associated with overtourism. Examples from Barcelona, Venice, Amsterdam, and Dubrovnik illustrated how destinations are responding through visitor management and restrictions on cruise tourism.

title: “What We Chose to Save” exhibition and Cultural Resilience Forum highlight Ukraine’s extraordinary cultural heritage rescue efforts
content:
On 2 October 2026, more than 150 Ukrainian and international heritage professionals, civil society representatives, military personnel and partners gathered in Kyiv for the Cultural Resilience Forum: From Emergency Response to a System of Protection.  A central highlight was the opening of the exhibition “What We Chose to Save: Stories from Cultural Rescue Missions in Ukraine,” which documents the people, decisions and efforts behind the protection of Ukraine’s cultural heritage amid Russia’s ongoing war.

Initiated by the Ukrainian Fulbright Circle, which operates the Europa Nostra Heritage Hub in Kyiv, the exhibition grew out of rescue missions carried out across Ukraine between 2022 and 2026. Developed in the frame of the the EU-funded European Heritage Hub and in collaboration with the Agency for Cultural Resilience (ACURE) and the Maidan Museum (Museum of the Revolution of Dignity), it brings together testimonies of those working to safeguard cultural heritage under extraordinary circumstances.

title: Hub’s high-level online Policy Talk sets the stage for further advocacy on cultural heritage and AI at the European level
content:
The European Heritage Hub Policy Talk “INNOVATE. PROTECT. EMPOWER. How cultural heritage can make Public AI a reality”, held online on 29 September 2026, drew strong global interest — gathering more than 280 attendees from around the world.

The online event, organised by Europeana as a digital partner of the Hub, explored what role the cultural heritage sector should play in the development, deployment and governance of AI. The discussion built on the Hub’s recently published policy paper, ‘Beyond adopter and supplier: putting cultural heritage at the heart of Europe’s Public AI ecosystem’, which sets out the policies and actions needed to make this vision a reality.

The Policy Talk also marked the launch of an advocacy campaign titled INNOVATE. PROTECT. EMPOWER. which calls on the European Commission to recognise the cultural heritage sector as a key partner in shaping Europe’s Public AI ecosystem, as it develops its forthcoming AI strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors, expected in 2027.

title: Hub publishes policy paper and launches campaign to put cultural heritage at the heart of Public AI in Europe
content:
The EU-funded European Heritage Hub has published its policy paper “Beyond adopter and supplier: putting cultural heritage at the heart of Europe’s Public AI ecosystem”, released on 29 September on the occasion of the Hub’s Policy Talk  “INNOVATE. PROTECT. EMPOWER: How cultural heritage can make Public AI a reality” and is launching its dedicated advocacy campaign. Developed with the Europeana Foundation and with input from Hub partners across Europe, the paper highlights the role of the cultural heritage sector in the European Commission’s forthcoming AI strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors, expected in 2027. The campaign turns its key messages into a call for action: organisations and networks across Europe are invited to endorse it.

Read the policy paper · Read the executive summary

The AI strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors was announced in the Culture Compass for Europe published in November 2025. The Hub’s paper builds on “The case for Public AI: making it happen with cultural heritage”, published in June 2026, and on the responses that the Hub and the Europeana Foundation submitted to the Commission’s Call for evidence.

title: Hub launches two new thematic task forces on music and digital heritage
content:
The European Heritage Hub is strengthening its role in advocacy and shaping European cultural policy with the launch of two new thematic task forces: the Music Task Force and the Digital Task Force. 

Coordinated by partners of the Hub together with members of the European Heritage Alliance, these Task Forces will connect experts with relevant stakeholders, bringing lessons and insights from the ground into European policy discussions and helping to ensure that European heritage voices are reflected in key policy developments.

Initiated by organisations including the European Union Youth Orchestra (EUYO), Centre Européen de Musique, European Early Music Network (REMA) and B’Rock Orchestra, the Music Task Force aims to champion music as a core component of European heritage, culture and public policy.

title: Hub had meetings at the European Parliament to advocate for a dedicated place and funding for culture and cultural heritage in future Horizon Europe and European Competitiveness Fund
content: As negotiations on the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) — the EU’s next long-term budget for 2028-2034 — continue, Europa Nostra, in its capacity as Project Leader of the European Heritage Hub, and representing the European Heritage Hub Consortium and the European Heritage Alliance, is stepping up the call for culture and cultural heritage to have a clearly recognised and adequately funded place in the EU’s future research, innovation and competitiveness programmes.

title: Culture as Democratic Infrastructure in a Changing Europe
content:
In Varietate Concordia — United in Diversity — captures one of Europe’s most enduring ambitions. Yet today, this principle is under increasing strain. Across the continent and beyond, societies are facing rising polarisation, declining trust in institutions, widening inequalities, rapid digital transformation, and the accelerating impacts of climate change. These pressures are not only political or economic — they are fundamentally relational. They shape how people perceive one another, how they interact, and how they imagine shared futures.

In this context, culture and heritage are often positioned as supportive or secondary policy domains. However, growing evidence suggests a different interpretation: culture and heritage function as critical democratic infrastructure. They shape the conditions under which democratic values are practiced, negotiated and sustained in everyday life (European Commission, 2023; Council of Europe, 2010). This article argues that culture should not be understood simply as a sector, but as an ecosystem of relationships and practices through which societies organise meaning, trust, identity and collective action.

title: The Living Past: Experimental Archaeology and Reenactment as a Shared Language for a Democratic Future
content:
Culture is a living process that belongs to everyone. Through more than twenty years of international experience in this field, I’ve seen how moving history out of textbooks and into the hands of the public can be a gamechanger. Living history and experimental archaeology go far beyond “reconstruction”: they are powerful, democratic tools that foster critical thinking and social cohesion. When you see a researcher sweating over a primitive forge or a weaver explaining an ancient technique, you’re looking at a shared language that everyone can understand, regardless of their background or education. It makes heritage inclusive in a way that academic lectures often can’t.

However, the quality of this “language” depends on the strength of our professional networks. A great example of this is the international Association of Experimental Archaeology, Open-Air Museums, Traditional Crafts, and Heritage Interpretation (EXARC). In its 25 years of work, it has shown how vital it is to connect open-air museums, universities, and practitioners. This kind of synergy is what keeps the field scientifically grounded.
